conceptTag: Why software gets cheaper per user
readerTitle: Why software gets cheaper per customer and cleaning doesn't
caseNote: 가상 사례 (홈 클리닝 회사, 일정 관리 앱, 기장 대행 회사) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 고객당 원가는 고정비가 퍼지면서 내려가지만, 결국 '한 명 더 서비스하는 비용(한계비용)'에서 멈춘다. 소프트웨어가 싸지는 이유는 규모 자체가 아니라 그 바닥이 낮기 때문이다.
misconception: 어떤 사업이든 고객이 늘면 소프트웨어처럼 고객당 원가가 계속 뚝뚝 떨어진다. 소프트웨어는 고객이 늘수록 추가 비용이 0이다.

sources.text: 미시경제학·관리회계의 표준 개념 (한계비용, 규모의 경제, 고정비·변동비 구분)

factChecks.note: 기장 대행: 고객당 월 6시간은 가상 수치. 실제 업계 평균 시간으로 쓰지 않도록 주의.

cards.title: Why software gets cheaper per customer and cleaning doesn't
body: Maria runs a home cleaning company. This year she doubled her clients, and her labor bill nearly doubled too.
The scheduling app she uses also doubled its customers this year. It hired almost no one. Same growth, very different costs.

image.label: A cleaning crew growing beside a phone app that stays the same size
image.brief: 화면 왼쪽: 청소 직원이 2명에서 4명으로 늘어나는 모습. 오른쪽: 같은 크기의 스마트폰 화면에 일정 앱, 주변의 작은 고객 아이콘만 늘어남. 실제 앱 로고나 상표는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: Maria's cost per clean
body: Maria pays $4,000 a month for her office, insurance and a scheduler. Each clean costs $85 in cleaner time and supplies.
She does 200 cleans a month and plans to reach 1,000. What happens to her cost per clean?

options.feedback: Her $4,000 does spread out, but every clean still needs $85 of labor and supplies. That **marginal cost** sets a floor.

options.text: It falls a little, then levels off near $85
options.feedback: Right. **Economies of scale** take her from $105 to $89 per clean. After that, the marginal cost of each clean is almost all that's left.
Close in spirit, since labor is most of her cost. But the fixed $4,000 does spread thinner, saving about $16 per clean.

cards.title: Cost per customer as each business grows
body: The app spends $50,000 a month on developers and design, whatever its size. Each extra customer adds about $3 for servers, card fees and support.

groups.label: Scheduling app: cost per customer per month

cards.callout: Same mechanism, different result. One more customer costs the app $3. One more clean costs Maria $85.

image.label: Cost per customer as each business grows
image.brief: Labeled HTML chart from the lesson numbers

cards.title: Two ideas explain the gap.
body: **Economies of scale:** cost per customer falls as fixed costs spread over more customers. Both businesses get this.
**Marginal cost:** what it costs to serve one more. It decides how far the fall can go. The app heads toward $3. Maria heads toward $85.
Software is the extreme case. Nearly all its costs are paid before the first customer arrives.

image.label: Two curves falling toward different floors
image.brief: 두 개의 하강 곡선. 위 곡선(청소)은 $85 점선 위에서 평평해지고, 아래 곡선(앱)은 $3 점선까지 거의 내려감. 각 점선에 "Cost of one more" 라벨.

cards.title: The app adds an AI assistant.
body: The app team wants to add an AI assistant. Each customer who uses it adds about $2 a month in computing costs. Prices stay the same.
How should they think about it?

options.text: Ignore it. Next to $50,000 in fixed costs, $2 is noise
options.feedback: At 50,000 customers, $2 is half the cost per customer. Once fixed costs are spread thin, **marginal cost** is most of what's left.

options.text: Treat it as a new floor: $3 becomes $5, so price or usage limits should reflect it
options.feedback: **Economies of scale** shrink the fixed part over time. Only pricing protects you from a growing per-customer part.

options.text: Drop it. Software should have no per-customer costs
options.feedback: Tidy, but the feature may be worth more than it costs. The question is whether the price covers the new marginal cost, not whether it's zero.

cards.title: Cheaper per customer isn't free.
body: Fixed costs keep growing. Apps need updates, security work and new features, so that $50,000 rarely stays put.
Some costs rise with size: support, sales teams for big clients, and custom requests from large accounts.
And lower cost per customer doesn't mean lower prices. It means each new customer adds more profit, as long as the price holds.

cards.title: Now it's a bookkeeping firm.
body: You do the books for 40 small businesses. Each client takes about 6 hours of bookkeeper time a month. You want to reach 400 clients.
What's the best path to a lower cost per client?

options.text: Hire ten times as many bookkeepers
options.feedback: You grow, but cost per client barely moves. Each client still brings 6 hours of **marginal cost**.

options.text: Build shared templates and automatic bank imports once, so each client needs fewer hours
options.feedback: You turn some per-client labor into a one-time fixed cost. Now **economies of scale** have something to spread, and the cost of one more client drops.

options.text: Cut prices now to win 400 clients fast, expecting costs to fall
options.feedback: This assumes software-style scale. With 6 hours of labor per client, costs won't fall much, and a low price could lose money on each one.

cards.softwareNote: This is how many service firms become software firms: they move work from each client into a tool built once.

cards.title: Cost per customer falls toward the cost of serving one more.
body: You used two ideas: **economies of scale** (fixed costs spread over more customers) and **marginal cost** (the cost of one more). Software gets cheaper per customer because its marginal cost is so low.
**Try it today:** split your monthly costs into what you pay regardless and what each customer adds. Your cost per customer can never fall below the second number.
